title: Manganese in Plants: What It Does and When Your Crop Needs It
metaTitle: Manganese in Plants: Role, Signs and When It Matters
metaDescription: Manganese in plants splits water in sunlight and switches on enzymes. See when each crop needs it, why limed soils run short, and how to supply it.
excerpt: Manganese in plants is the helper that splits water inside the leaf, the first step of turning sunlight into food. It also switches on enzymes that build defenses against disease. A crop short of it gets speckled, pale young leaves. Here is what it does, when each crop needs it most and why heavily limed soils often run short.

heroImage.alt: Leaf with pale, speckled areas between the veins: manganese in plants running short

blocks.text:
In the leaf, manganese sits in the part of the chloroplast that splits water in sunlight and releases oxygen. Without it photosynthesis stalls at the very first step.

Manganese also switches on enzymes that make lignin, the tough stuff in cell walls, and other compounds that help the plant fight fungi and other diseases. So a crop short of it grows weak and catches more disease.
A helper, needed in small amounts

Manganese is a helper. It works inside enzymes and the water splitting step without being used up, so crops need only a few hundred grams per hectare.

Like iron, it is usually in the soil but in the wrong form. Oxygen and a high pH turn it into forms the roots cannot take, while flooding and acid soil free it, sometimes too much.

blocks.caption: Manganese in short
rows: The young leaves, speckled between the veins

blocks.text:
Manganese moves poorly, so the shortage starts on the young and middle leaves. They turn pale between the veins with small dead specks, and the plant may look grayish. It looks a lot like iron shortage, but the speckles and the paler veins give manganese away.

See [manganese deficiency](/nutrient-deficiencies/manganese-deficiency) for the signs crop by crop.
When manganese in plants is most critical

Manganese matters most for upland crops on limy or heavily limed soil, early in the season. Flooded palay seldom lacks it because flooding frees manganese.

DAT means days after transplanting, DAS days after sowing in the field, and DAP days after planting. The days are the usual ones for a typical variety, so a long or short variety moves them a little. Timing manganese in plants to these windows gets more harvest from the same bags. Our guide to [fertilizer timing by growth stage](/blog/fertilizer-timing-by-growth-stage) puts them together for a whole season.

blocks.text: What keeps manganese from the crop

A pH above about 6.5, heavy liming, dry and well aired soil, and soil rich in organic matter all bind manganese. On the other hand, strongly acid and waterlogged soil can free so much that it harms the crop.

So the risk of shortage is highest on a limed, sandy or limy upland field in a dry spell.

Manganese sulfate on the soil or as a leaf spray is the usual fix. A spray works faster on limy soil, where soil applied manganese locks up quickly. Many trace element blends also carry it. See [micronutrients for rice](/blog/micronutrients-for-rice).

items: Manganese sulfate: on the soil or as a leaf spray.
Trace element blends and foliar fertilizers: small amounts with zinc, iron and copper.

blocks.title: Too much manganese is toxic on acid soil
blocks.text: On very acid or waterlogged soil, manganese can rise to toxic levels and show as brown spots on older leaves. Liming acid soil to the right pH fixes it.

items.q: How do I tell manganese from iron deficiency?
items.a: Both pale the young leaves between the veins. Manganese adds small dead specks and the veins look paler, while iron leaves the veins sharp green.
